solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Drugged competitors grappling with spectators

indicators.note: wrestlers grappling get their arms around something, so one word wraps around the others

blocks.note: people who vie with each other
W is the standard abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: Athletes high on drugs are wrestling with the crowd watching them.
explanation.walkthrough: W and E sit inside the word for competitors, splitting it after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Viewers are people who watch, the same as an audience of onlookers.

clue.text: A sucker pushed around by a daily

definitions.text: A sucker pushed around by a daily

blocks.note: surface: a gullible person being bullied
setter's reading: a machine that sucks dust, pushed about by a daily, British slang for a cleaning lady

explanation.surface: A gullible victim bullied by a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' suggests a newspaper, but in Britain a daily is also a domestic cleaner who comes in each day.
explanation.definitionFit: A household appliance that sucks up dust, pushed over carpets by whoever does the housework.

clue.text: Retired show-off or another still at it?

explanation.surface: A former poser, or one who still flaunts himself?
explanation.walkthrough: Read as EX-POSER, a former show-off; read as one word, an exposer is a show-off who is still at it.
explanation.definitionFit: An exposer is a person who exposes or reveals things, including himself, a flasher still in action.

clue.text: Dismiss and deny? Don't start that!

indicators.note: without a start means the opening letter of that word goes

explanation.surface: An exasperated person telling someone not to start rejecting and denying things.
explanation.definitionFit: To eject someone is to throw them out, the same as dismissing them.

clue.text: Nurses go crazy for them

indicators.note: crazy means wild and disordered, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Hospital nurses swoon over the doctors who operate.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: the medical-drama cliché of nurses infatuated with operating doctors.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgeons are the doctors who operate, the stock heart-throbs of hospital romance.

clue.text: Method of payment inspection for auditors

indicators.note: auditors are, literally, listeners, so the word is taken by ear rather than by spelling

explanation.surface: An auditor examines how a firm pays its bills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditors' wants to mean accountants, which fits the money surface; here it means people who hear.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheque is a written order to a bank to pay someone, one way of settling a bill.

clue.text: Minister's aide in old vehicle going round university?

indicators.note: going round something encircles it, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: a crate is slang for an old car

explanation.surface: A clergyman's assistant in a rickety car drives round a campus.
explanation.definitionFit: A curate is an assistant to a parish priest, helping the minister of a church.

clue.text: City-focused character

blocks.note: EC is the postcode for the City of London

explanation.surface: Someone whose whole personality revolves around the financial City.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district, whose postcodes start EC.
explanation.definitionFit: A character in the informal sense is an odd, colourful person, which is an eccentric.

clue.text: Idealistic union with Scottish foreman?

blocks.note: a top Ian: the man at the fore with a typical Scottish name

explanation.surface: A dreamy trade union with a Scot as its foreman.
explanation.walkthrough: Fore-man is read as foremost man, a top man, and Ian is the stock Scottish first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Utopian describes visionary schemes for a perfect society, which is idealistic.

clue.text: Career working around fancy pub?

indicators.note: a machine that is working is in motion, so these letters get moved about
fancy means elaborate or decorated, signalling these letters dressed up in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone whose job keeps them busy in a smart bar.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a job spent working around drink is the cupbearer's.
explanation.definitionFit: A cupbearer was the servant who poured and served wine at a royal or noble table.

clue.text: Disease setting back men in sporting contest

indicators.note: setting something back turns it the other way, so the letters run right to left
in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: OR, other ranks, the ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: An illness stops a team's players taking part in a tournament.
explanation.definitionFit: Croup is a childhood respiratory infection that causes a barking cough.

clue.text: A funny peddler turned in sensational work

indicators.note: turned means changed around, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A comic street seller performs in a melodramatic piece.
explanation.walkthrough: A penny dreadful was a cheap, lurid Victorian serial magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: Penny dreadfuls were sensational popular fiction sold for a penny, so a sensational work.

clue.text: Put out all but the first of a bitch's litter?

indicators.note: everything except the opening letter is kept, so the front is dropped

blocks.note: a set of pups, which a female dog gives birth to

explanation.surface: Someone is distressed when almost all of a dog's puppies are given away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bitch' is the proper term for a female dog; her litter is a pup set.
explanation.definitionFit: Put out is an idiom for annoyed or disturbed, the adjective sense of upset.

clue.text: Switched racket to draw 10-10 in time added on

indicators.note: things switched have swapped places, so these letters are put in another order

blocks.note: ten in words, then X, ten in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A tennis player changes racket with the score tied at ten-all in extra time.
explanation.walkthrough: The tennis picture makes racket a bat, but it is noise; 10-10 supplies ten twice in two forms.
explanation.definitionFit: An extension is extra time granted beyond a deadline or the normal span of play.

clue.text: Find fault with unit housing hot blower in motor

indicators.note: a housing encloses what it holds, so the following item goes inside

blocks.note: H for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Someone complains about a car's heater unit.
explanation.walkthrough: CARP and ONE together house H. Blower is British slang for a telephone.
explanation.definitionFit: A car phone is a telephone fitted in a vehicle, and blower is slang for telephone.

clue.text: A chap with lots of potential — Wellington's captain?

definitions.text: A chap with lots of potential

blocks.clueFragment: A chap with lots of potential
blocks.note: first meaning: an ambitious person likely to go far
second meaning, whimsical: the pilot of a Wellington bomber flies high

explanation.walkthrough: Wellington suggests the Iron Duke, but the Vickers Wellington was a Second World War bomber, whose captain literally flew high.
explanation.definitionFit: A promising, ambitious person is called this, and an airman aloft is one in the literal sense.

clue.text: Up for it, having got behind a bit of bulldog spirit

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a small piece, here its opening letter
one part comes after the other, so it is placed second

explanation.surface: Keen and ready, someone backs the British bulldog spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bulldog spirit' reads as British grit, but spirit alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Brandy is a spirit distilled from wine.

clue.text: Rugby player in nude shot made widely available

indicators.note: shot means ruined or worn out, so these letters are broken up and rearranged
in puts one piece inside another

blocks.note: a lock is a second-row forward in rugby

explanation.surface: A naked photograph of a rugby player gets circulated everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' wants to be a photograph in this surface; it signals the letters of nude are mangled.
explanation.definitionFit: Unlocked describes something opened up so that anyone can get at it.

clue.text: Zip fastener gymnast displays around the middle

indicators.note: what is shown is in the centre of the phrase, its letters running across the word gap

blocks.note: inside the two words, spanning the gap

explanation.surface: A gymnast's costume has a zip fastener around the waist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zip fastener' reads as one thing; Zip alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Zip means vigour or liveliness, a synonym for energy.

clue.text: Having snorted a bit of cocaine, left in high spirits

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a small part, its first letter
snorting takes something in, so one piece goes inside another

explanation.surface: After a line of cocaine, someone departs on a high.
explanation.definitionFit: Excited means thrilled and lively, a synonym for being in high spirits.

clue.text: Small cab rank storms buffet at the roadside

indicators.note: something that storms rages wildly, so these letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: S for small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A tiny taxi queue gets battered by storms beside the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A snack bar is a counter selling light food, here a roadside café.

clue.text: Pit housing Corbynite surge according to Spooner

indicators.note: Spooner was famed for swapping the opening sounds of words, so the initial sounds trade places

blocks.note: a follower of the left-wing Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn is a red

explanation.surface: A political surge of Corbyn supporters engulfs a coal mine.
explanation.walkthrough: Red boom, with the first sounds exchanged, becomes the answer. Pit is British slang for bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Pit is slang for bed, and the room that houses your bed is the bedroom.

clue.text: One smashed at overseas wedding beginning to rile cook?

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: plates are smashed at Greek weddings

explanation.surface: Breaking a dish at a foreign wedding begins to annoy the caterer.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a whimsical definition: a cook who plates up dishes.
explanation.definitionFit: A plater is one who plates food, arranging it for serving, as a cook does.

clue.text: A sporting swinger with nothing on can start to lift party

indicators.note: in a down-free reading 'on' puts one part straight after another
the start of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: can and nick are both slang for prison
FA, short for sweet FA, means nothing

explanation.surface: A sports fan with no clothes on can be seen lifting the party mood.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick Faldo is an English golfer who won six major titles. Nothing goes after NICK.
explanation.definitionFit: Faldo is a golfer, and a golfer swings a club, so he is a sporting swinger.

clue.text: Army doctor with answer for cold organs

indicators.note: one thing put for another means a letter is swapped out and replaced

blocks.note: a medic is a military doctor
C for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A military doctor answers questions about cold-damaged body parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organs' looks anatomical in this medical surface; it means newspapers and broadcasters.
explanation.definitionFit: Organs are publications or channels voicing views, and the media are such outlets collectively.

clue.text: Hectic last quarter for Balearic Isle heads

indicators.note: only the final fourth of that word is kept, the rest dropped
heads means leads or goes in front, so one part is placed first

blocks.note: eight letters, so a quarter is two

explanation.surface: A busy final quarter for the leaders of a Balearic island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balearic Isle' wants to be Majorca or Ibiza; the isle is Man, which heads the last two letters of Balearic.
explanation.definitionFit: Manic means frenzied and frantically busy, a synonym for hectic.

clue.text: Elegant royal relations and two unknowns

blocks.note: R for royal, as in RN
it is slang for sex, sexual relations
Z and Y are unknowns in algebra

explanation.surface: A smart royal family with a couple of nobodies among them.
explanation.walkthrough: The odd count (1,2,2) mirrors the pieces; 'relations' looks like family but means sexual relations.
explanation.definitionFit: Ritzy means luxurious and smart, after the opulent Ritz hotels.

clue.text: A royal nursed by nob beginning to do well

indicators.note: something nursed is held in the arms, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: a toff is a posh person

explanation.surface: A young prince being looked after by an aristocrat starts to thrive.
explanation.walkthrough: Nob and toff are British words for an upper-class person.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking off is an idiom for suddenly becoming successful, like a plane lifting into the air.

clue.text: One who loves to strip lady, lord and serf

indicators.note: stripping removes the outer layer, leaving only the inner letters of each word

explanation.surface: A lecher enjoys undressing people of every social class.
explanation.definitionFit: An adorer is a devoted admirer, someone who loves deeply.

clue.text: Editor backing new claim of Number Ten

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the word is read in the opposite direction
a new version is a remake, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A journalist supports a fresh assertion made by Downing Street.
explanation.walkthrough: Number Ten is Downing Street, the British Prime Minister's home; here it is just the number ten.
explanation.definitionFit: Decimal describes a counting system based on ten.
